title: Gayatri Mantra

{{short description|Mantra of the Vedic tradition}} {{Use British English|date=June 2015}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2018}} [[File:Gayatri-mantra-devanagari.png|thumb|Gāyatrī [[Mantra]] in the [[Devanāgarī]] script, with symbols for Vedic pitch accent]] [[File:Gayatri Mantra as it is 2021 02 13 05 48 +.wav|thumb|Recitation of the Gayatri mantra. Duration: 23 seconds.]] {{Hinduism}} [[File:Gayatri1.jpg|thumb|Gayatri Mantra personified as the goddess [[Gayatri]], surrounded by the [[Tamil language|Tamil]] ''[[Om]]'' symbol, with the mantra written in it. From left clockwise: [[Matrikas|Brahmi]] as ''Pratah Sandhya'' (Morning), [[Matrikas|Maheshwari]] as ''Madhyanika Sandhya'' (Afternoon), Pranava Rishi and [[Matrikas|Vaishnavi]] as ''Sayam Sandhya'' (Evening).]] The '''Gāyatrī Mantra''' ({{IPA|sa|ɡaː.jɐ.triː.mɐn.trɐ.}}), also known as the '''Sāvitrī Mantra''' ({{IPA|sa|saː.vi.triː.mɐn.trɐ.}}), is a sacred [[mantra]] from the ''Ṛig [[Veda]]'' ([[Mandala 3]].62.10), dedicated to the Vedic deity [[Savitr]].{{Cite web|title=Rig Veda: Rig-Veda, Book 3: HYMN LXII. Indra and Others.|url=https://www.sacred-texts.com/hin/rigveda/rv03062.htm|access-date=2020-09-29|website=www.sacred-texts.com}}{{cite book |last1=Haas |first1=Dominik |title=Gāyatrī: Mantra and Mother of the Vedas |date=2023 |publisher=Austrian Academy of Sciences Press |location=Vienna |isbn=978-3-7001-9391-3 |url=https://doi.org/10.1553/978OEAW93906}} The mantra is attributed to the [[brahmarshi]] [[Vishvamitra]]. The term '''Gāyatrī''' may also refer to a ''type'' of mantra which follows the same [[Vedic metre]] as the original '''Gāyatrī Mantra''' (without the first line). There are many such Gāyatrīs for various gods and goddesses.Swami Vishnu Devananda, Vishnu Devananda (1999). ''Meditation and Mantras'', p. 76. Motilal Banarsidass Publ. Furthermore, {{IAST|'''[[Gāyatrī]]'''}} is the name of the Goddess of the mantra and the meter.{{cite journal|last=Staal|first=Frits|date=June 1986|title=The sound of religion|journal=Numen|volume=33|issue=Fasc. 1|pages=33–64 |jstor=3270126|doi=10.1163/156852786X00084}} The Gayatri mantra is cited widely in Hindu texts, such as the mantra listings of the [[Śrauta]] liturgy, and classical Hindu texts such as the ''[[Bhagavad Gita]]'',{{sfn|Rahman|2005|p=300}}{{sfn|Radhakrishnan|1994|p=266}} ''[[Harivamsa]]'',{{sfn|Vedas|2003|p=15–16}} and ''[[Manusmṛti]]''.{{sfn|Dutt|2006|p=51}} The mantra and its associated metric form was known by the Buddha.{{cite journal|last1=Shults|first1=Brett|title=On the Buddha's Use of Some Brahmanical Motifs in Pali Texts|journal=Journal of the Oxford Centre for Buddhist Studies|date=May 2014|volume=6|page=119|url=http://jocbs.org/index.php/jocbs/article/view/76/96}} The mantra is an important part of the initiation ceremony. Modern Hindu reform movements spread the practice of the mantra to everyone and its use is now very widespread.{{sfn|Rinehart|2004|p=127}}{{sfn|Lipner|1994|p=53}} ==Dedication== {{See also|Surya}} The ''Gāyatrī'' mantra is dedicated to [[Savita (deity)|Savita]], a [[solar deity]]. The mantra is attributed to the much revered sage [[Viśvāmitra]], who is also considered the author of Mandala 3 of the Rigveda.Constance Jones, James D. Ryan (2005), ''Encyclopedia of Hinduism'', Infobase Publishing, p.167, entry "Gayatri Mantra"Roshen Dalal (2010), ''The Religions of India: A Concise Guide to Nine Major Faiths'', Penguin Books India, p.328, entry "Savitr, god" ==Text== The main mantra appears in the hymn [[Mandala 3|RV 3]].62.10. During its recitation, the hymn is preceded by ''{{IAST|[[om|oṃ]]}}'' ({{lang|sa|ॐ}}) and the formula ''{{IAST|bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ}}'' ({{lang|sa|भूर् भुवः स्वः}}), known as the ''{{IAST|mahāvyāhṛti}}'', or "great (mystical) utterance". This prefixing of the mantra is properly described in the [[Aranyaka#Taittiriya Aranyaka|''Taittiriya Aranyaka'']] (2.11.1-8), which states that it should be chanted with the syllable ''{{IAST|oṃ}}'', followed by the three Vyahrtis and the Gayatri verse.{{cite book |author1=Carpenter, David Bailey |author2=Whicher, Ian |title=Yoga: the Indian tradition |publisher=Routledge |location=London |year=2003 |page=31 |isbn=0-7007-1288-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HlPta3a38P0C&pg=PA31}} Whereas in principle the ''gāyatrī'' mantra specifies three [[Pada (foot)|''pāda''s]] of eight syllables each, the text of the verse as preserved in the Samhita is one short, seven instead of eight. Metrical restoration would emend the attested tri-syllabic ''{{IAST|vareṇyaṃ}}'' with a tetra-syllabic ''{{IAST|vareṇiyaṃ}}''.B. van Nooten and G. Holland, ''Rig Veda. A metrically restored text''. Cambridge: Harvard Oriental Series (1994).[http://www.utexas.edu/cola/centers/lrc/RV/RV03.html#3.062.10a] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408082331/http://www.utexas.edu/cola/centers/lrc/RV/RV03.html#3.062.10a|date=8 April 2016}} The Gayatri mantra with ''[[svara]]s'': {{Verse transliteration-translation|ॐ भूर्भुव॒: स्व॒: तत्स॑वि॒तुर्वरे॑ण्यं॒ भर्गो॑ दे॒वस्य॑ धीमहि। धियो॒ यो न॑: प्रचो॒दया॑त्॥|oṃ bhūrbhuva̱: sva̱: tatsa̍vi̱turvare̍ṇya̱ṃ bhargo̍ de̱vasya̍ dhīmahi. dhiyo̱ yo na̍: praco̱dayā̍t.{{cite web | title=rv03.062 | website=sanskrit-lexicon.github.io | url=https://sanskrit-lexicon.github.io/rvlinks/rvhymns/rv03.062.html#rv03.062.10 | language=qu | ref={{sfnref | sanskrit-lexicon.github.io}} | access-date=2024-04-13}}|{{interlinear | indent = 2 | lang1 = sa-Latn|tat savituḥ vareṇyam bhargaḥ devasya dhīmahi dhiyaḥ yaḥ naḥ pra-codayāt|that [[Savitr]]-GEN lovely-ACC splendor-ACC god-GEN may-we-attain thoughts-ACC who-NOM our may-he-guide|'May we attain that lovely splendor of the [[Rigvedic deities|God]] Savitā, who may guide our thoughts.'}}|lang=sa|originalHeading=[[Devanagari]]|translationHeading=[[Gloss (annotation)|Gloss]]|transliterationHeading=[[IAST]]}} == Translations == The Gayatri mantra has been translated in many ways.{{cite journal |last1=Haas |first1=Dominik A. |title=Translating the Gāyatrī-Mantra |journal=Asian Literature and Translation |date=2023 |volume=10.1 |pages=47–91 |doi=10.18573/alt.57}} Quite literal translations include: * [[Swami Vivekananda]]: "We meditate on the glory of that Being who has produced this universe; may He enlighten our minds."{{cite book|last=Vivekananda|first=Swami|title=The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda|publisher=Advaita Ashram|year=1915|page=211|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=030TAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA211}} * [[Monier Monier-Williams]] (1882): "Let us meditate on that excellent glory of the divine vivifying Sun, May he enlighten our understandings."{{cite book|author= Monier Monier-Williams|title=The Place which the Ṛig-veda Occupies in the Sandhyâ, and Other Daily Religious Services of the Hindus|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x3gOAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA164|year=1882|publisher=A. Asher & Company|location=Berlin|page=164}}{{cite book|editor=Forrest Morgan|others=et al|title=The Bibliophile Library of Literature, Art and Rare Manuscripts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qb8CAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA14|volume=1|year=1904|publisher=The International Bibliophile Society|location=New York|page=14}} * [[Ralph T.H. Griffith]] (1896): "May we attain that excellent glory of [[Savitr|Savitar]] the god: So may He stimulate our prayers."{{cite book|last=Griffith|first=Ralph T. H.|title=The Hymns of the Rigveda|publisher=E.J. Lazarus|year=1890|pages=87|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gZURAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA87}} * [[S. Radhakrishnan]]: :* (1947): "We meditate on the effulgent glory of the divine Light; may he inspire our understanding." :* (1953): "We meditate on the adorable glory of the radiant sun; may She inspire our intelligence."S. Radhakrishnan, ''[[The Principal Upanishads (book)|The Principal Upanishads]]'', (1953), p. 299 * [[Sri Aurobindo]]: "We choose the Supreme Light of the divine Sun; we aspire that it may impel our minds."{{cite book |title=Evening talks with Sri Aurobindo |year=2007 |publisher=Sri Aurobindo Ashram, Publication Dept |isbn=978-81-7058-865-8 |pages=58–59 |edition=4th rev.}} Sri Aurobindo further elaborates: "The Sun is the symbol of divine Light that is coming down and Gayatri gives expression to the aspiration asking that divine Light to come down and give impulsion to all the activities of the mind." * [[Stephanie W. Jamison]] and Joel P. Brereton: "Might we make our own that desirable effulgence of god Savitar, who will rouse forth our insights."{{cite book|author=Stephanie Jamison|title=The Rigveda –– Earliest Religious Poetry of India|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1LTRDwAAQBAJ|year=2015|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0190633394|page=554}} More interpretative translations include: * [[Sir John Woodroffe]] (Arthur Avalon) (1913): "Om. Let us contemplate the wondrous spirit of the Divine Creator (''Savitri'') of the earthly, atmospheric, and celestial spheres. May He direct our minds (that is, 'towards' the attainment of ''dharmma'', ''artha'', ''kama'', and ''moksha''), Om."{{cite book|last=Woodroffe|first=John|title=Tantra of the Great Liberation (Mahānirvāna Tantra)|publisher=Dover Publications, Inc.|year=1972|page=xc}} * [[Ravi Shankar (poet)]]: "Oh manifest and unmanifest, wave and ray of breath, red lotus of insight, transfix us from eye to navel to throat, under canopy of stars spring from soil in an unbroken arc of light that we might immerse ourselves until lit from within like the sun itself."{{cite web|url=https://thepunchmagazine.com/the-byword/poetry/world-poetry-prose-portfolio-tokya-tanka-and-other-poems|title=GAYATRI MANTRA |first=Ravi |last=Shankar |author-link=Ravi Shankar |date=January 2021 }} * [[Shriram Sharma|Pandit Shriram Sharma]]: Om, the Brahm, the Universal Divine Energy, vital spiritual energy (Pran), the essence of our life existence, Positivity, destroyer of sufferings, the happiness, that is bright, luminous like the Sun, best, destroyer of evil thoughts, the divinity who grants happiness may imbibe its Divinity and Brilliance within us which may purify us and guide our righteous wisdom on the right path.{{cite book|last=Sharma|first=Shriram|title=Meditation on Gayatri mantra |publisher=AWGP Organization |url=http://www.awgp.org/spiritual_wisdom/gayatri/importance_of_gayatri_mantr/meaning_meditation_on_gayatri_matr }} * [[William Jones (philologist)|Sir William Jones]] (1807): "Let us adore the supremacy of that divine sun, the god-head who illuminates all, who recreates all, from whom all proceed, to whom all must return, whom we invoke to direct our understandings right in our progress toward his holy seat."{{cite book|last=Jones|first=William|title=The works of Sir William Jones|publisher=J. Stockdale and J. Walker|year=1807|volume=13|page=367|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w9QMAAAAYAAJ}} * [[William Quan Judge]] (1893): "Unveil, O Thou who givest sustenance to the Universe, from whom all proceed, to whom all must return, that face of the True Sun now hidden by a vase of golden light, that we may see the truth and do our whole duty on our journey to thy sacred seat."{{cite web|url=http://www.blavatsky.net/theosophy/judge/articles/commentary-on-the-gayatri.htm |title=A COMMENTARY ON THE GAYATRI |first=William |last=Judge Quan |author-link=William Quan Judge |work=The Path |date=January 1893 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100614051043/http://www.blavatsky.net/theosophy/judge/articles/commentary-on-the-gayatri.htm |archive-date=14 June 2010 }} * [[Sivanath Sastri]] ([[Brahmo Samaj]]) (1911): "We meditate on the worshipable power and glory of Him who has created the earth, the nether world and the heavens (i.e. the universe), and who directs our understanding."Appendix "C", Sivanath Sastri "History of the Brahmo Samaj" 1911/1912 1st edn. page XVI, publ. Sadharan Brahmo Samaj, 211 Cornwallis St. Calcutta, read : {{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.33057/page/n343/mode/2up|title= History Of The Brahmo Samaj Vol. 1 : Sastri, Sivanath-Internet Archive|year= 1911}}. Retrieved on 23 November 2020.{{refn|group=note|The word Savitr in the original Sanskrit may be interpreted in two ways, first as the sun, secondly as the "originator or creator". Raja [[Ram Mohan Roy]] and Maharshi [[Debendranath Tagore]] used that word in the second sense. Interpreted in their way the whole formula may be thus rendered.}} * [[Sivananda Saraswati|Swami Sivananda]]: "Let us meditate on Isvara and His Glory who has created the Universe, who is fit to be worshipped, who is the remover of all sins and ignorance. May he enlighten our intellect." * [[Dayananda Saraswati]] (founder of [[Arya Samaj]]): "Oh God! Thou art the Giver of Life, Remover of pain and sorrow, The Bestower of happiness. Oh! Creator of the Universe, May we receive thy supreme sin-destroying light, May Thou guide our intellect in the right direction."{{cite web|url=http://www.aryasamaj.com/enews/2010/dec/3.htm|title=MEDITATING ON GAYATRI MANTRA}} * [[Kirpal Singh]]: "Muttering the sacred syllable 'Aum' rise above the three regions, And turn thy attention to the All-Absorbing Sun within. Accepting its influence be thou absorbed in the Sun, And it shall in its own likeness make thee All-Luminous."{{cite book|last=Singh|first=Kirpal|title=The Crown of Life|year=1961|page=275|url=https://www.ruhanisatsangusa.org/pdf/CrownofLife2012.pdf}} ===Syllables of the Gayatri mantra=== Gayatri mantra, called ''Gayatri Chandas'' in Sanskrit, is twenty-four syllables comprising three lines (Sk. ''padas'', literally "feet") of eight syllables each, in this case starting from ''tat savitur vareṇyaṃ''. The first line, oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, is not part of the gayatri syllables, but an introduction to invoke the mantra to work on three Vyāhṛti or planes (physical, mental and spiritual).{{cite book |last1=Williams |first1=Monier |title=A Sanskrit–English Dictionary, […], new edition |date=1899 |publisher=Oxford: At the Clarendon Press |page=1039 }} The Gayatri mantra as received is short one syllable in the first line: ''{{IAST|tat sa vi tur va reṇ yaṃ}}''. Being only twenty-three syllables the Gayatri mantra is ''Nichruth Gayatri Chandas'' ("Gayatri mantra short by one syllable"). {{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}A reconstruction of ''{{IAST|vareṇyaṃ}}'' to a proposed historical ''{{IAST|vareṇiyaṃ}}'' restores the first line to eight syllables. In practise, people reciting the mantra may retain seven syllables and simply prolong the length of time they pronounce the "m", they may append an extra syllable of "mmm" (approximately va-ren-yam-mmm), or they may use the reconstructed ''{{IAST|vareṇiyaṃ}}''.{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}} ==Textual appearances== ===Hindu literature=== The Gayatri mantra is cited widely in Hindu texts, such as the mantra listings of the [[Śrauta]] liturgy,{{refn|group=note|Sama Veda: 2.812; Vajasenayi Samhita (M): 3.35, 22.9, 30.2, 36.3; Taittiriya Samhita: 1.5.6.4, 1.5.8.4, 4.1.11.1; Maitrayani Samhita: 4.10.3; Taittiriya Aranyaka: 1.11.2}}{{refn|group=note|Where it is used without any special distinction, typically as one among several stanzas dedicated to Savitar at appropriate points in the various rituals.}} and cited several times in the Brahmanams and the Srauta-sutras.{{refn|group=note|Aitareya Brahmana: 4.32.2, 5.5.6, 5.13.8, 5.19.8; Kausitaki Brahmana: 23.3, 26.10; Asvalayana Srautasutra: 7.6.6, 8.1.18; Shankhayana Srautasutra: 2.10.2, 2.12.7, 5.5.2, 10.6.17, 10.9.16; Apastambha Srautasutra: 6.18.1}}{{refn|group=note|In this corpus, there is only one instance of the stanza being prefixed with the three mahavyahrtis.VSM.36.3 This is in a late supplementary chapter of the Shukla Yajurveda samhita, listing the mantras used in the preliminaries to the [[pravargya]] ceremony. However, none of the parallel texts of the pravargya rite in other samhitas have the stanza at all. A form of the mantra with all seven vyahrtis prefixed is found in the last book of the [[Taittiriya Aranyaka]], better known as the [[Mahanarayana Upanishad]].Dravida recension: 27.1; Andhra recension: 35.1; Atharva recension: 15.2 It is as follows:
ओम् भूः ओम् भुवः ओम् सुवः ओम् महः ओम् जनः ओम् तपः ओम् स॒त्यम्।       ओम् तत्स॑वि॒तुर्वरे॑ण्य॒म् भर्गो॑ दे॒वस्य॑ धीमहि।
      धियो॒ यो नः॑ प्रचो॒दया॑त्।
      ओमापो॒ ज्योती॒ रसो॒ऽमृतं॒ ब्रह्म॒ भूर्भुव॒स्सुव॒रोम्।}} It is also cited in a number of grhyasutras, mostly in connection with the [[upanayana]] ceremonyShankhayana grhyasutra: 2.5.12, 2.7.19; Khadira grhyasutra: 2.4.21; Apastambha grhyasutra: 4.10.9-12; Varaha grhyasutra: 5.26 in which it has a significant role{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. The Gayatri mantra is the subject of esoteric treatment and explanation in some major [[Upanishads]], including [[Mukhya Upanishads]] such as the [[Brihadaranyaka Upanishad]],{{refn|group=note|6.3.6 in the well-known Kanva recension, numbered 6.3.11-13 in the Madhyamdina recension.}} the [[Shvetashvatara Upanishad]]{{refn|group=note|4.18}} and the [[Maitrayaniya Upanishad]];{{refn|group=note|6.7, 6.34, albeit in a section known to be of late origin.}} as well as other well-known works such as the [[Jaiminiya Upanishad Brahmana]].{{refn|group=note|4.28.1}} The text also appears in minor Upanishads, such as the [[Surya Upanishad]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}} The Gayatri mantra is the apparent inspiration for derivative "gāyatrī" stanzas dedicated to other deities{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. Those derivations are patterned on the formula {{IAST|''vidmahe'' - ''dhīmahi'' - ''pracodayāt''"}},Ravi Varma(1956), p.460f, Gonda(1963) p.292 and have been interpolatedKeith, Vol I. p.lxxxi into some recensions of the [[Shri Rudram Chamakam|Shatarudriya]] litany.{{refn|group=note|Maitrayani Samhita: 2.9.1; Kathaka Samhita: 17.11}} Gāyatrīs of this form are also found in the Mahanarayana Upanishad.{{refn|group=note|Taittiriya Aranyaka: 10.1.5-7}} The Gayatri mantra is also repeated and cited widely in Hindu texts such as the ''[[Mahabharata]]'',{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}} ''[[Harivamsa]]'',{{sfn|Vedas|2003|p=15–16}} and ''[[Manusmṛti]]''.{{sfn|Dutt|2006|p=51}} === Buddhist corpus === In [[Majjhima Nikaya]] 92, the Buddha refers to the Sāvitri (Pali: ''sāvittī'') mantra as the foremost meter, in the same sense as the king is foremost among humans, or the sun is foremost among lights: {{blockquote|''aggihuttamukhā yaññā sāvittī chandaso mukham; Rājā mukhaṃ manussānaṃ, nadīnaṃ sāgaro mukhaṃ. Nakkhattānaṃ mukhaṃ cando, ādicco tapataṃ mukhaṃ; Puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānānaṃ, saṅgho ve yajataṃ mukhan.'' The foremost of sacrifices is offering to the sacred flame; the Sāvittī is the foremost of poetic meters; of humans, the king is the foremost; the ocean’s the foremost of rivers; the foremost of stars is the moon; the sun is the foremost of lights; for those who sacrifice seeking merit, the Saṅgha is the foremost.{{cite book|last1=Bikkhu|first1=Sujato|title=Majjhima Nikaya translated by Bhikkhu Sujato|date=2018|url=https://suttacentral.net/mn92/en/sujato}}}} In [[Sutta Nipata]] 3.4, the Buddha uses the Sāvitri mantra as a paradigmatic indicator of Brahmanic knowledge: {{blockquote|''Brāhmaṇo hi ce tvaṃ brūsi, Mañca brūsi abrāhmaṇaṃ; Taṃ taṃ sāvittiṃ pucchāmi, Tipadaṃ catuvīsatakkharaṃ'' If you say you brahmin are, but call me none, then of you I ask the chant of Sāvitrī, consisting of three lines in four and twenty syllables.{{cite book|last1=Mills|first1=Laurence|title=To Sundarika-Bhāradvāja on Offerings|date=2020|url=https://suttacentral.net/snp3.4/en/mills}}}} [[File:Gayatri japa.jpg|thumb|Gayatri [[Japa]], 1851 lithograph]] ===Upanayana ceremony=== Imparting the Gayatri mantra to young [[Hindu]] men is an important part of the traditional [[upanayana]] ceremony{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}, which marks the beginning of study of the Vedas. [[Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan]] described this as the essence of the ceremony,{{cite book|last=Radhakrishnan|first=Sarvepalli|title=Religion and Society|year=1947|page=135|publisher=Read Books |isbn=9781406748956|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SFNE0x5HFLMC&pg=PA135}} which is sometimes called ''"Gayatri [[diksha]]"'', i.e. initiation into the Gayatri mantra.{{cite journal|last=Wayman|first=Alex|title=Climactic Times in Indian Mythology and Religion|journal=History of Religions|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|volume=4|issue=2|jstor=1061961|year=1965|pages=295–318|doi=10.1086/462508|s2cid=161923240}} However, traditionally, the stanza RV.3.62.10 is imparted only to Brahmana{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. Other Gayatri verses are used in the upanayana ceremony are: RV.1.35.2, in the [[tristubh]] meter, for a kshatriya and either RV.1.35.9 or RV.4.40.5 in the jagati meter for a Vaishya.This is on the authority of the Shankhayana Grhyasutra, [http://www.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe29/sbe29035.htm 2.5.4-7] and 2.7.10. J. Gonda, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/1580265 "The Indian mantra"], ''Oriens'', Vol. 16, (31 December 1963), p. 285 ===Mantra-recitation=== Gayatri [[japa]] is used as a method of [[prāyaścitta]] (atonement){{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. It is believed by practitioners that reciting the mantra bestows wisdom and enlightenment, through the vehicle of the Sun ([[Savitr]]), who represents the source and inspiration of the universe. ===Brahmo Samaj=== In 1827 [[Ram Mohan Roy]] published a dissertation on the Gayatri mantraTitle of the text was ''Prescript for offering supreme worship by means of the Gayutree, the most sacred of the Veds''. {{cite book|last=Roy|first=Rammohun|title=Translation of Several Principal Books, Passages and Texts of the Veds, and of Some Controversial Works on Brahmunical Theology: and of some controversial works on Brahmunical theology. |publisher=Parbury, Allen, & co.|year=1832|url=https://archive.org/details/translationseve00roygoog|page=[https://archive.org/details/translationseve00roygoog/page/n125 109]}} that analysed it in the context of various [[Upanishads]]. Roy prescribed a Brahmin to always pronounce ''om'' at the beginning and end of the Gayatri mantra.{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/theenglishworks01rammuoft/theenglishworks01rammuoft_djvu.txt|title = Prescript for offering supreme worship by means of the Gayutree, the most sacred of the Veds|first = Ram Mohan| last = Roy| year = 1901| publisher = Kuntaline press| quote= So, at the end of the Gayutree, the utterance of the letter Om is commanded by the sacred passage cited by Goonu-Vishnoo 'A Brahman shall in every instance pronounce Om, at the beginning and at the end; for unless the letter Om precede, the desirable consequence will fail; and unless it follow, it will not be long retained.'}} From 1830, the Gayatri mantra was used for private devotion of [[Brahmo]]s{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. In 1843, the First Covenant of [[Brahmo Samaj]] required the Gayatri mantra for Divine Worship{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. From 1848 to 1850 with the rejection of Vedas, the [[Adi Dharma]] Brahmins use the Gayatri mantra in their private devotions.Sivanath Sastri "History of the Brahmo Samaj" 1911/1912 1st edn. publ. Sadharan Brahmo Samaj, 211 Cornwallis St. Calcutta ===Hindu revivalism=== In the later 19th century, Hindu reform movements spread the chanting of the Gayatri mantra.{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}} In 1898 for example, [[Swami Vivekananda]] claimed that, according to the Vedas and the ''Bhagavad Gita'', a person became Brahmana through learning from his [[Guru]], and not because of birth{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}}. He administered the Gayatri mantra to non-Brahmins in Ramakrishna Mission.{{cite book|last=Mitra |first=S. S.|title=Bengal's Renaissance|publisher=Academic Publishers|page=71|isbn=978-81-87504-18-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WPFeBY9YEAQC&pg=PA71|year=2001}} This Hindu mantra has been popularized to the masses, pendants, audio recordings and mock scrolls.{{cite book|last=Bakhle|first=Janaki|title=Two men and music: nationalism in the making of an Indian classical tradition|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|page=293|isbn=978-0-19-516610-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=daPoKY6a-p0C&pg=PA293}} Various Gayatri yajñas organised by All World Gayatri Pariwar at small and large scales in late twentieth century also helped spread [https://www.saregama.com/song/gayatri-mantra_89069 Gayatri mantra] to the masses.{{cite book|last=Pandya|first=Dr. Pranav|title=Reviving the Vedic Culture of Yagya|publisher=Vedmata Gayatri Trust|year=2001|pages=25–28}} ===Indonesian Hinduism=== The Gayatri Mantra forms the first of seven sections of the [[Trisandya|Trisandhyā Puja]] (Sanskrit for "three divisions"), a prayer used by the Balinese Hindus and many [[Hinduism in Indonesia|Hindus in Indonesia]]. The Gāyatrī Mantra (Sanskrit pronunciation: [ɡaː.jɐ.triː.mɐn.trɐ.]), also known as the Sāvitrī Mantra (Sanskrit pronunciation: [saː.vi.triː.mɐn.trɐ.]), is a sacred mantra from the Ṛig Veda (Mandala 3.62.10), dedicated to the Vedic deity Savitr. The mantra is attributed to the brahmarshi Vishvamitra.
The term Gāyatrī may also refer to a type of mantra which follows the same Vedic metre as the original Gāyatrī Mantra (without the first line). There are many such Gāyatrīs for various gods and goddesses. Furthermore, Gāyatrī is the name of the Goddess of the mantra and the meter.
The Gayatri mantra is cited widely in Hindu texts, such as the mantra listings of the Śrauta liturgy, and classical Hindu texts such as the Bhagavad Gita, Harivamsa, and Manusmṛti. The mantra and its associated metric form was known by the Buddha. The mantra is an important part of the initiation ceremony. Modern Hindu reform movements spread the practice of the mantra to everyone and its use is now very widespread.
